summary: This experimental memo defines Candidate Access Router Discovery. A mobile device uses it to learn which nearby access routers could take over its connection and what they can do, before a handover begins.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a wireless device can move its connection to another router, it needs to know which routers are nearby and what each can offer. RFC 4066 defines the messages for finding that out. The device asks its current router, which looks up the answers and returns the candidate routers' addresses and capabilities, sometimes after asking the candidate routers themselves.

subtitle: Lets a device find out which nearby routers it could move to, and what each of them offers.

tldr.problem: A mobile device cannot choose which router to move to until it knows which routers are nearby and what services each of them offers.
tldr.mechanism: The device sends the link-layer identifiers it can hear to its current router, which answers with the IP addresses of the candidate routers and their capabilities. Routers also exchange candidate information among themselves over SCTP, secured with IPsec.
tldr.outcome: The device can compare the candidates before a handover and pick one whose capabilities match what it needs. The document is Experimental.

facts.label: Inter-router transport (AR-AR)
facts.value: SCTP, with IPsec securing AR-AR messages

facts.label: Request retry
facts.value: 2 seconds, doubling, giving up after 15 seconds

today: RFC 4066 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the allocation rules in RFC 4065 and on Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 in RFC 4068, and the document itself notes that the kinds of access network where CARD would be useful are not yet widely deployed or measured.

sections.title: What Candidate Access Router Discovery Does
sections.content:
IP mobility protocols such as Mobile IP let a mobile node hand its connection over from one access router to another. Work on seamless handover needs the node to know the candidate access routers it could be transferred to, before the handover starts. The act of finding them has two parts: identifying their IP addresses, and finding out their capabilities. That act is called candidate access router discovery, or CARD.

A mobile node often has a choice of candidate routers. It picks one by matching its own requirements against what each candidate offers. The document is careful to leave that decision algorithm out of scope; it defines the protocol that supplies the information the decision needs. The problem statement for candidate router discovery is recorded separately, and the appendices describe two ways of building the table that maps an access point's link-layer identifier to the address of the router behind it, which is what makes reverse address translation possible. The default method is static configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol answers two questions for a device that is about to move: which routers could take over, and what can each of them do? Deciding which one to pick is left to the device.

sections.title: The Two Functions of CARD
sections.content:
The first function is reverse address translation. A wireless device can hear the link-layer identifiers of nearby access points while it scans, before it has decided to hand over. Each such identifier belongs to an access point, and behind that access point sits a router with an IP address. The device cannot work out that address on its own, so it sends the identifier to its current router, and the current router returns the IP address of the router associated with that access point.

The second function is discovery of candidate router capabilities. Information about what a candidate router offers helps the device make a good handover decision, and it feeds the target router selection algorithm. Some capability parameters are static and others change over time. The definition of the capabilities themselves is out of scope for this document; what the document does specify is how they are encoded and how they are carried.
sections.plainLanguage: Two jobs. The first is turning a nearby access point's hardware address into the IP address of the router behind it. The second is collecting what each candidate router can do, such as how much bandwidth it has.

sections.title: How the Protocol Runs
sections.content:
The device sends a CARD Request to its current router, naming the access point identifiers it heard while scanning. If it wants capabilities as well as addresses, it sets the C-flag in the request; without that flag the router does only the reverse address translation. The request may also carry a Preferences parameter, naming the capability attributes the device cares about, or a Requirements parameter, giving attribute and value pairs such as a quality-of-service constraint, so the router can send back only the candidates that meet them.

The current router looks the identifiers up in a table that maps access point identifiers to router IP addresses. The table is configured statically by default and may be populated dynamically. In the reply the router returns the IP addresses of the candidate routers, each candidate's identifiers, and, when asked, the associated capabilities. The status code on each identifier says what happened: CANDIDATE when the router sent every candidate it knows about because the request named no identifier, MATCH when an identifier resolves to a router that was already named in the same reply, and RESOLVER ERROR when the router could not resolve it at all. A context identifier ties the identifier, the address and the capability information together even though they travel in separate sub-options.

The device picks a random sequence number for the request, and the router repeats it in every message of the reply. If no reply arrives within the retry interval, the device retransmits with exponential backoff, keeping the same sequence number, until a response arrives or the retry limit is reached. Routers also exchange candidate information with each other over the inter-router interface: a router sends a CARD Request to a peer when its own table entries time out, and the peer answers with a CARD Reply. A candidate router may also send an unsolicited reply when its own capabilities change.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks its current router to look up the access points it can hear. The router answers with the addresses and capabilities of the routers behind them, and marks each answer so the device can tell which candidate it belongs to. Routers also keep each other up to date about neighbouring candidates.

sections.title: The CARD Messages and Sub-Options
sections.content:
The interface between the device and its current router uses ICMP for transport. Because an ICMP message fits in a single packet and ICMP has no way of retransmitting a packet if the signalling is lost, CARD adds its own rules for transport performance. The device should limit how much it asks for in one packet, since ICMP has no fragmentation above the IP level. The main header has an ICMP type, a code of 0, a checksum, a subtype for CARD and a reserved field that the sender must set to zero and the receiver must ignore.

Messages carry options, and options carry sub-options. Every option has a type, a length counted in units of 8 octets, and a 3-bit version field, which is 1 for this specification. The CARD Request option adds a set of flags, a sequence number and the sub-options. The mandatory sub-options are the Layer-2 ID, the Capability Container, the Address, the Trusted Anchor and the Router Certificate. The Preferences and Requirements sub-options are optional. Sub-option lengths are also counted in units of 8 octets and aligned on a 64-bit boundary, with shorter sub-options padded with null octets.

Capabilities travel as attribute and value pairs inside the Capability Container sub-option. Each pair has an AVP code, of which 0x0000 is reserved, a length, a reserved field and a lifetime in seconds. A static capability must set the lifetime to the maximum value, which means it never expires, and a lifetime of zero deletes a capability entry. The Address sub-option carries the candidate router's IP address, with an address type of 0x01 for IPv4 and 0x02 for IPv6, and its length is 1 unit for IPv4 and 3 units for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are ICMP packets carrying options, and the options carry pieces: which access point was heard, which router it belongs to, and what that router can do. Every message has a random number in it, so the device can match the answer to its question and ignore anything else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Messages between routers must be authenticated, because an attacker who can modify them can change the capability information, and the messages should also be encrypted when the traffic crosses the public Internet and confidentiality is needed. Two routers must use IKE to negotiate an IPsec ESP security association for authentication, and a second one for encryption when confidentiality is required. Replay protection should be enabled as well. The memo does not recommend using CARD between administrative domains until the policy questions that raises are better understood.

Between the device and its current router, the router must authenticate the CARD Reply messages, because a bogus router could send information that leads the device to hand over to a fake router and lose its traffic. IKE is not the right tool for that link, since setting up an IPsec security association there is likely to be a performance problem, so the SEND security association is used instead and the router must include a SEND signature option in its replies. Requests are not authenticated, because they carry no information the router has to trust; the asymmetry is the same as in IPv6 router discovery.

Two further protections are described. A router can be flooded with requests, so it should rate limit them and start dropping messages at random once the rate is exceeded, and the device must discard replies for which it has no outstanding request. The same discard rule protects the device against replayed replies, and on the router side replay protection should be enabled in the IKE negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The router-to-router messages must be signed and are usually encrypted, so a stranger cannot feed the network false information. The device checks that the answers come from the router it is really talking to, because handing over to a fake router would lose the device's traffic.

messages.label: AR-AR CARD Request
messages.note: Sent when the current router's table entries time out.

messages.label: AR-AR CARD Reply
messages.note: The peer answers with the requested information.

messages.label: MN-AR CARD Request
messages.note: The device passes on the access point identifiers it heard while scanning.

messages.label: MN-AR CARD Reply
messages.note: The candidate addresses, their identifiers and, if asked, their capabilities.

items.label: L2 ID
items.desc: The link-layer identifier of an access point. Mandatory.

items.label: Address
items.desc: The resolved IP address of a candidate router. Mandatory.

items.label: Capability Container
items.desc: The capabilities of one candidate router, as attribute and value pairs. Mandatory.

items.label: Preferences
items.desc: The attributes the requester is interested in. Optional.

items.label: Requirements
items.desc: Attribute and value pairs the requester requires. Optional.

items.label: Trusted Anchor
items.desc: The name of a trusted anchor for which the requester holds a certificate. Mandatory.

items.label: Router Certificate
items.desc: One certificate from a certification path. Mandatory.
